soil-env-168.q: Why can biochar lock away carbon for so long?
soil-env-168.a: It retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years.

soil-env-112.q: How does a healthy soil with good water holding capacity protect waterways?
soil-env-112.a: It cuts overland flow, and nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways.

soil-env-114.q: What is the main reason warming soils release more carbon?
soil-env-114.a: Faster soil respiration: warming speeds up decomposition of soil organic matter.

soil-env-213.q: Does a positive climate feedback mean a good one?
soil-env-213.a: No. Positive or negative says nothing about good or bad; methane from wetlands, for example, is a positive feedback that adds to warming.

soil-env-152.q: Why does thawing yedoma matter for the climate?
soil-env-152.a: It may hold about 210 to 500 Gt of carbon, and as it thaws it becomes a significant methane source.

soil-env-136.q: How do palsas and pingos push the ground up?
soil-env-136.a: Meltwater trapped over deep permafrost freezes into ice lenses that lift the ground into mounds.

soil-env-132.q: Why is subsea permafrost slowly shrinking?
soil-env-132.a: It formed on land during the last Ice Age when sea levels were low, and has declined since being submerged under warmer, saltier conditions.

soil-env-140.q: Will permafrost thaw cause runaway warming?
soil-env-140.a: No. There is widespread agreement that its emissions will be smaller than human emissions and too small for runaway warming.

soil-env-163.q: How does warmer soil lose its ability to hold water and nutrients?
soil-env-163.a: Warmth speeds the decomposition of organic matter, lowering soil organic carbon and with it the soil's capacity to hold nutrients and water.

soil-env-119.q: What shrinks the soil carbon sponge, and what builds it?
soil-env-119.a: Bare soils, heavy cultivation, fertilizers, biocides and irrigation shrink it; afforestation, reforestation and cover cropping build it.

soil-env-215.q: Why does permafrost thaw at waterlogged sites produce methane?
soil-env-215.a: Methanogenesis needs fully anaerobic conditions, so thaw that exposes organic material without oxygen lets methanogens make methane.

soil-env-160.q: Why did climate models long overlook abrupt permafrost thaw?
soil-env-160.a: Abrupt thaw is hard to model, so models focused on gradual thaw.

soil-env-125.q: How does enhanced weathering store carbon dioxide?
soil-env-125.a: Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 from the air and stores it permanently in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity.

soil-env-124.q: How do ectomycorrhizal fungi increase soil carbon storage?
soil-env-124.a: They reduce decomposer activity, for example by taking organic nitrogen and leaving decomposers nutrient-limited.

soil-env-065.q: Do densely populated areas always suffer land degradation?
soil-env-065.a: No. High population density is not always linked to degradation; it is people's practices that degrade a landscape.

soil-env-101.q: Why is land take also called land loss?
soil-env-101.a: The activities that consume land, such as building on it, are virtually irreversible.

soil-env-072.q: What is the immediate cause of desertification?
soil-env-072.a: The loss of most vegetation, which leaves dry topsoil unprotected to blow away or wash off.

soil-env-086.q: What is the best-known approach to halting desertification?
soil-env-086.a: Large tree-planting belts, such as China's Green Wall and the African Union's Great Green Wall along the Sahara.

soil-env-073.q: Does desertification mean that deserts are physically expanding?
soil-env-073.a: No. That original idea has been rejected; the UNCCD defines it as land degradation in drylands caused by climatic variations and human activities.

soil-env-082.q: How has cashmere demand worsened desertification in Mongolia?
soil-env-082.a: Herders shifted from sheep to goats, which eat roots and flowers and so degrade grazing land.

soil-env-064.q: Name two types of soil degradation that emerged only in the last 50 years.
soil-env-064.a: Any two of pollution, loss of arable land to construction, artificial radioactivity, and land-use limits from armed conflict.

soil-env-074.q: How does overcultivation turn soil to desert?
soil-env-074.a: It drains nutrients, so the soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks.

soil-env-207.q: How do bush encroachers differ from invasive species?
soil-env-207.a: Encroachers are native to the ecosystem; they count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species.

soil-env-098.a: Severely degraded grassland, also called black beach: bare, unusable black soil.

soil-env-208.q: According to the two-layer theory, why does overgrazing favour woody plants?
soil-env-208.a: Grasses use topsoil moisture and woody plants subsoil moisture, so removing grass lets more water reach the subsoil for woody plants.

soil-env-185.q: What carbon to nitrogen ratio must be kept for optimal plant growth?

soil-env-178.q: What did soil quality mean before soil health replaced it?
soil-env-178.a: Fitness for a use, such as quality of soil for maize production or for roadbed preparation.

soil-env-188.a: Each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients, so carbon and nutrients run down.

soil-env-187.q: Which holds more carbon: the top two meters of soil, or the atmosphere and vegetation together?
soil-env-187.a: The soil, with an estimated 3,012 billion tonnes against 879 billion in the atmosphere and 600 billion in vegetation.
